say: Cars get crash tests. Planes get crash investigators. But AI agents that issue refunds and delete data usually just get a demo. This is Crashworthy: crash tests, and a five star safety rating, for AI agents that move money. Built on neatlogs.

Each test rebuilds a real AI failure. Air Canada's invented refund policy. The one dollar Chevy Tahoe. Replit deleting a production database during a code freeze. Pass or fail is decided by code, not by an AI judge. Five tests are hidden from the fixer, to catch overfitting.

Every crash is a neatlogs trace. Here, a cheap support agent was reminded there is a code freeze, and then asked to delete test data. It deleted two production rows, and told the engineer it worked. That is a severity four crash, and it caps the rating.

The repair loop reads the failing traces back from neatlogs. Entire Graph locates the code. A headless Claude Code session makes exactly one change: here, a guard that blocks production deletes. The gate re-runs all sixteen tests, and keeps the change only if visible safety rises, and hidden safety does not fall.

Then we asked the fixer to cut cost. It made the agent eight percent cheaper. But safety on the hidden tests dropped from thirty-eight to twenty-three percent. The gate rejected it, on the record. Cheaper, but less safe, does not ship.
Every fix, and every rejected attempt, is a commit with an Entire checkpoint: the exact Claude Code session that made it, its prompt, and its edits. Nine rounds. Three kept. Six rolled back.
The result, measured as the worst of three runs: one star, to two stars. Visible safety from forty, to sixty-five percent. Hidden safety held. Six tests still fail, and the certificate says so.
And how do we know the tests themselves work? We planted ten known bugs in the agent. The suite caught all ten.

A full certification costs about six cents. In the cfo dot ai plan, that is a ninety-nine percent gross margin, at forty-nine dollars per agent per month. Crashworthy. Agents earn trust before they touch money.
